feature: The timeline of an hour-long edit: scrolling and zooming
summary: Scrolling along the hour-long reference edit's timeline went from about half a second a frame to about 50 ms, because the timeline now builds only the clips, cuts and gaps near what is on screen. Zooming near the whole-edit view is still slow (about 570 ms a frame), so this task stays open.
setup: Photonz Probe built by Scripts/probe-app.sh, release Next, no flag changed from its default. The 60 minute reference edit: Scripts/perf/reference-edit.sh 60.

try.do: Run Scripts/perf/reference-edit.sh 60 and wait for the edit to open.
Pinch the timeline in until about a minute shows, then two-finger scroll along it end to end.
Pinch back out to the whole hour and watch how the timeline keeps up.
Press Space and watch the playhead run along the zoomed-in timeline.
Trim the end of a clip ahead of the playhead while it plays, then press Command-Z.

evaluate: Does scrolling along the zoomed-in hour feel smooth enough to work in now?
Is zooming out to the whole hour slow enough that you would avoid doing it?
Does the timeline look exactly as it did before at every zoom (clips, cuts, gaps, ticks)?
Are the stacked Zoom lanes under V1 (one per zoomed clip) something you want gone on long edits?
measured: Measured with a timeline walk on the 60 minute reference edit (524 clips, 377 cuts, 126 zooms), the speed walk's timeline, idleBuilds and edits measures, on this Mac at 120 Hz.

Before, as the speed walk used to measure it (with the walk's own markers hung, about 29,000 AppKit views in the window): zoom in 1225 ms a frame, zoom out 1099 ms, scroll 901 ms; edits while playing, longest main thread pass: trim 833 ms, move 780 ms, blade 977 ms, undo 837 ms.

The speed walk now takes the walk's markers down for every speed measure, as a person's app has none (374 AppKit views in the window). Before any timeline change, measured that way: zoom in 736 ms a frame, zoom out 747 ms, scroll 554 ms.
After: zoom in 571 ms a frame (p95 650), zoom out 580 ms (p95 759), scroll 50 ms (p95 59, worst 68). No frame meets 8.3 ms yet.
After, edits while playing, longest main thread pass: trim 559 ms, move 492 ms, blade 696 ms, undo 713 ms (bar: 16 ms).
Playing with nothing edited: 93 new pictures in 3 s (the clock's full rate; 70 before), and clip bars built per new picture: 0 before and after; only the panel's Time section, 0.01 a picture.

Where a zoom frame's time goes now (sample, main thread): about 70% SwiftUI's graph upkeep for the ~500 clip views on screen at the whole-hour view, about 18% their bodies; the layer-by-id search (13% before) and the hold-drift walk per bar are gone from the profile.
rough: Zooming near the whole-hour view is still about 570 ms a frame: every clip is on screen there, so building only what is in sight does not help. The next step, still this task's: draw clips too narrow to grab as one painted layer per track instead of a view each.

Edits on the hour-long edit still hold the main thread 0.5 to 0.7 s against the 16 ms bar; the cause is the same graph upkeep after a document write that a-long-edit-with-transitions-plays-scrubs-and-ed names for the 6 minute edit.

Every zoomed clip gets its own Zoom lane under its track, so the hour-long edit stacks 126 near-empty lanes; they did not show as a cost in the profile, but they push everything below them out of sight. Filed as a-long-edit-with-many-zooms-shows-one-zoom-lane.

Every speed walk number before 2026-11-14 was measured with the walk's markers hung, which made timeline numbers about half again slower than a person's app; the short walk's baseline was not rewritten, since it only fails on a worse number.
